turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Margaret Doyle? In you come. I'll do your checks before the doctor, he's running a bit behind.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Grand, love. The Naas Road was a nightmare, we sat there a good twenty minutes not moving.
[SEG0003] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I said we'd miss the worst of it if we left after nine, but sure listen.
[SEG0004] person_1 (NURSE): Blood pressure is 152 over 88, pulse 76, oxygen 98 percent. Pop up on the chair when you're ready.
[SEG0005] person_2 (PATIENT): 152, Janey. Would the tea I had in the car put that up, do you think?
[SEG0006] person_1 (NURSE): Doctor will talk you through it. I'll be just outside.
[SEG0007] person_4 (DOCTOR): Sorry, this yoke is frozen again. Margaret, yes? What brings you in?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): Ah just a check-up, doctor. I'm not one for darkening the door over nothing.
[SEG0009] person_4 (DOCTOR): A check-up. Say that again, sorry, I was clicking the wrong window. What sort of check-up?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): The usual, make sure I'm still ticking. I'm 67, it's no harm to be looked at.
[SEG0011] person_2 (PATIENT): Did you see the weather though? Lashing when we left, and by Tallaght the sun was splitting the stones.
[SEG0012] person_4 (DOCTOR): Mmm. One second, it's asking me for the password again.
[SEG0013] person_2 (PATIENT): My grandson Cillian had hurling in that wet yesterday, under-12s, skidding all over the pitch. He got a point in the second half, we were all delighted.
[SEG0014] person_3 (CAREGIVER): The gear was destroyed, Margaret. Muck up to the knees.
[SEG0015] person_2 (PATIENT): And the jersey is still in the sink. His mother says it'll never be white. They have Lucan next week if the pitch isn't a swamp.
[SEG0016] person_4 (DOCTOR): Right, I'm with you now. The match, fair play to him. You're in for a check-up, so.
[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): That's the size of it. Nuala brought me, she's my home help in the mornings.
[SEG0018] person_4 (DOCTOR): Any particular bother, or is it the blood pressure we're minding?
[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): The blood pressure, mostly. I've had that for years, since I was about sixty. I take the tablet for it.
[SEG0020] person_3 (CAREGIVER): It's been there a long time, doctor. You'd have it in the chart.
[SEG0021] person_4 (DOCTOR): Yes, hypertension, ongoing, I can see it here. The tablet — which one? The list has jumped.
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): The blood pressure tablet. Ramipril. I take it every morning. I think the dose is 5 milligrams.
[SEG0023] person_4 (DOCTOR): 5, you said? Sorry, say the dose again, I was typing over you.
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): 5 milligrams, I'm nearly sure. The small white ones.
[SEG0025] person_3 (CAREGIVER): The box at home says 10 milligrams, doctor. One every morning. She can't read the label without the glasses.
[SEG0026] person_4 (DOCTOR): We won't guess it so, the dose is up in the air. Anything else you're taking?
[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): Baby aspirin. They told me one a day for the heart, 75 milligrams, but I only take it on and off. Some weeks I forget the thing entirely.
[SEG0028] person_3 (CAREGIVER): The blister pack is still half full at the end of the month, I've seen it.
[SEG0029] person_4 (DOCTOR): On and off, noted. Did you stop any tablet, or is there one you were given and never took?
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): I stopped the water tablet in March. The frusemide. It had me up and down to the toilet all night, so I left it off.
[SEG0031] person_4 (DOCTOR): Frusemide, stopped in March. And a cholesterol tablet, were you started on one?
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): Atorvastatin. They wrote the script last year but I never took a single tablet. I didn't fancy starting it, and the chemist can keep it.
[SEG0033] person_4 (DOCTOR): If you never took it, it doesn't go on the list. Any allergies to medicines?
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Nothing. No allergies at all.
[SEG0035] person_3 (CAREGIVER): She's never said a word about an allergy to me.
[SEG0036] person_4 (DOCTOR): Good. Any chest pain? Pain in the chest itself?
[SEG0037] person_2 (PATIENT): No. No chest pain. I'm grand on that score.
[SEG0038] person_4 (DOCTOR): Not when you walk, or coming up the stairs at home?
[SEG0039] person_2 (PATIENT): Ah I wouldn't call it pain, doctor. Pain is what my sister had, this isn't that.
[SEG0040] person_3 (CAREGIVER): She stops halfway up the stairs, though. I've watched her grab the banister and wait.
[SEG0041] person_4 (DOCTOR): Margaret, say that again, I had my head in the screen. What happens on the stairs?

[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): Well, actually, there's a tight feeling in the chest when I climb the stairs, or if I walk fast. Not a pain exactly, more a band across it. It eases off if I stop for a minute.
[SEG0043] person_4 (DOCTOR): How long have you had that tightness?
[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): A couple of months. Two, maybe. I wouldn't swear to it.
[SEG0045] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Longer, Margaret. It was there before Christmas, that's nearly six months.
[SEG0046] person_2 (PATIENT): Was it? I couldn't put a date on it if you paid me.
[SEG0047] person_4 (DOCTOR): So somewhere between two and six months. We won't nail the start today.
[SEG0048] person_4 (DOCTOR): Does the tightness come when you're sitting down, at rest?
[SEG0049] person_2 (PATIENT): No, never at rest. Only the stairs or if I'm hurrying.
[SEG0050] person_4 (DOCTOR): Sweating with it? A sick feeling? Pain going down the arm?
[SEG0051] person_2 (PATIENT): No sweating, no sick feeling, and it doesn't go down the arm. Just the band, and then it's gone.
[SEG0052] person_4 (DOCTOR): Cough, or trouble with the breathing apart from that?
[SEG0053] person_2 (PATIENT): No cough. The breathing is grand once I've stopped.
[SEG0054] person_2 (PATIENT): My sister had a stent put in, down in Cork, a couple of years back. She was a smoker her whole life. I never smoked, not once.
[SEG0055] person_4 (DOCTOR): Sorry, the sister — say that again, I opened the letters tab by mistake.
[SEG0056] person_2 (PATIENT): My sister had a stent. And I never smoked a day in my life, that's the bit I was saying.
[SEG0057] person_3 (CAREGIVER): She lives on her own in the bungalow. I come three mornings a week.
[SEG0058] person_4 (DOCTOR): Lives alone, home help three mornings. Any chest pain at night?
[SEG0059] person_2 (PATIENT): No. I sleep fine, no pain at night.
[SEG0060] person_4 (DOCTOR): Let me have a listen... Lungs are clear, the heart sounds are normal, and there's no swelling at the ankles.
[SEG0061] person_2 (PATIENT): Ah that's something. I had myself half thinking of the sister, God love her.
[SEG0062] person_4 (DOCTOR): For a plain check-up I'd book a chest x-ray and bloods for the cholesterol and the kidneys, and leave it there.
[SEG0063] person_4 (DOCTOR): Actually, no, forget the chest x-ray. With that tightness on the stairs we'll do an ECG, and bloods for cholesterol and kidney function.
[SEG0064] person_2 (PATIENT): An ECG, the stickers? My sister was full of those.
[SEG0065] person_4 (DOCTOR): The very thing. We'll get the ECG done before you go, and the bloods after.
[SEG0066] person_1 (NURSE): I can take her for the ECG when you're finished, and the bloods are at phlebotomy down the hall.
[SEG0067] person_4 (DOCTOR): This sounds like it could be angina, that exertional tightness, but that's only a working impression until the ECG and the bloods are back.
[SEG0068] person_2 (PATIENT): Angina. And I only came in for a check-up. Typical.
[SEG0069] person_3 (CAREGIVER): One thing at a time. We'll hear what the tests say.
[SEG0070] person_4 (DOCTOR): If the tightness comes, stop and rest. If it starts while you're sitting, or there's sweating or that sick feeling, go to the emergency department, don't sit on it.
[SEG0071] person_2 (PATIENT): Stop and rest, and the hospital if I'm sitting down and it comes. Right.

[SEG0072] person_4 (DOCTOR): And please take the baby aspirin, the 75, every day the way it was prescribed, not on and off. Keep taking the ramipril every morning as well until we confirm the strength.
[SEG0073] person_2 (PATIENT): I'll park the aspirin by the kettle. The ramipril is with the breakfast, I don't miss that one.
[SEG0074] person_4 (DOCTOR): Come back in a fortnight and we'll go through the results together.
[SEG0075] person_2 (PATIENT): A fortnight. Do I ring, or will there be a card?
[SEG0076] person_4 (DOCTOR): Reception will book the fortnight. That's a definite visit, not a maybe.
[SEG0077] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I'll have her here. Mornings are easier, once breakfast is done.
[SEG0078] person_2 (PATIENT): If Cillian has a match that morning we might be tight for time, but we'll make the fortnight.
[SEG0079] person_4 (DOCTOR): The form wants a tick. Any trouble with the waterworks or the bowels?
[SEG0080] person_2 (PATIENT): No, waterworks are fine and the bowels are grand. Not a bother there.
[SEG0081] person_1 (NURSE): Whenever you're set, Margaret, I'll bring you round for the ECG.
[SEG0082] person_2 (PATIENT): Grand so. Thanks for seeing me, even with that computer acting the maggot.
[SEG0083] person_4 (DOCTOR): We'll sort it. Easy on the stairs until we know where we stand.

spec.situation: Man or woman 50-70 who comes 'for a check-up' and only slowly admits a tight feeling in the chest when climbing stairs or walking fast; first denies chest pain, later describes the tightness. Takes a BP tablet and aspirin on and off. Doctor orders ECG and bloods.
features: tangent_small_talk: a long tangent or small talk (traffic, cricket, the weather, a grandchild) that holds NO clinical content; nothing from it is extracted.
doctor_changes_mind: the doctor says one plan, then changes it after new information; the label holds the final plan.

stopped_or_never_taken: a medicine the patient stopped, was never given or only took once ('I stopped it in March'). Status discontinued, not current; a medicine never taken is not recorded as a medication.

colloquial_drug_names: medicines referred to by colour, purpose or brand ('the water tablet', 'Crocin', 'my sugar tablets', 'the purple inhaler'); the name is recorded as said, the normalized name only if it is clear.
spec.doctor_style: distracted by the computer, asks for repeats

bad.reason: Drug, dose, indication supported; frequency wrong—patient says prescribed daily but actually takes it on and off.
bad.text: baby aspirin (generic_name=aspirin, dose=75 mg, frequency=once a day, indication=heart, status=currently_used, reported_by=patient)

omissions.text: Ramipril dose is disputed: patient said she thinks it is 5 mg, but caregiver said the home box says 10 mg once every morning; doctor decided not to guess and said the strength needs confirming.
Aspirin adherence detail: patient said she only takes the 75 mg baby aspirin on and off and some weeks forgets it entirely; caregiver said the blister pack is still half full at the end of the month.
Frusemide was stopped by the patient in March because it had her up and down to the toilet all night.
Atorvastatin was prescribed last year but the patient never took a single tablet because she did not want to start it.
Chest pain was specifically denied when asked: patient said no chest pain, including no pain when walking or climbing stairs, before later clarifying it was chest tightness rather than pain.
No shortness of breath/breathing trouble apart from the exertional chest tightness; patient said breathing is grand once she has stopped.
Doctor briefly considered a chest X-ray for a plain check-up, then explicitly cancelled that plan and changed to ECG plus bloods because of the exertional chest tightness.
ECG was to be done before the patient left that day, and bloods afterwards at phlebotomy down the hall.
Safety-net advice included going to the emergency department if the tightness starts while sitting at rest, or if there is sweating or a sick feeling; patient repeated back the at-rest advice.
Doctor advised to keep taking ramipril every morning until the strength is confirmed.
Follow-up booking detail: reception will book the fortnight appointment and the doctor emphasized it is a definite visit, not optional.
